hero.name: Sunita
hero.who: a 35-year-old staff nurse in Lucknow who works extra shifts yet never feels ahead

story.b: Sunita is a staff nurse at a private hospital in Lucknow. Most weeks she takes two extra shifts on top of her regular ones. Her days are twelve hours long, and her feet ache on the auto ride home. On the first of the month her salary arrives. By the twentieth it is gone. Rent, her son's school fees, the fridge instalment, auto fares, food orders after night duty, and a new phone she bought after a terrible week on the ward. She has almost no free time and almost no money left, and she cannot quite say where either of them went. Her sister asks why she looks so tired. Sunita says she is just busy.

ask.q: Sunita works more hours than ever and still runs out of money by the twentieth. What should she question first?
o: How to get even more extra shifts each month
Which credit card gives her the most cashback
What her money is actually costing her, in hours of her life
ask.why: More shifts trade even more of her life for money that keeps vanishing, and cashback is a tiny fix. The deeper question is the real trade she is making. Seeing what money costs in time changes how she earns and how she spends it.

chapters.take: Money is not free. You pay for it with hours of your life.

story.b: Sunita has been eyeing a large smart TV. It costs thirty-two thousand rupees, and the shop near Hazratganj offers easy instalments. Before deciding, she does a small sum on the back of a duty roster. She works out roughly what one hour of her work earns. The TV comes to about three long night shifts. She pictures those nights: the beeping monitors, the call bells, the cold tea at three in the morning. The old TV at home still works fine. She decides to wait. The next week she does the same with a dress she likes. It is about four hours. She buys that one, happily, because those four hours feel worth it.

ask.q: Sunita's colleague wants an expensive handbag after a hard week. What question fits this idea best?
o: Is it on sale this weekend?
How many hours of her working life will this bag cost?
Will her friends notice and admire it?
ask.why: A sale only changes the price tag, and admiration fades fast. Converting the price into hours of work shows the real trade she is making. Sometimes the bag will still feel worth it, but now she chooses with open eyes.

chapters.take: Before buying, ask how many hours of your life it costs.

story.h: The real price of a night
story.b: Sunita is offered yet another extra night shift, and her first instinct is to say yes. Then she sits down with a notebook and adds up what a night shift really costs her. The late auto home is more expensive than the morning one. After nights she orders food because she is too tired to cook. The next day mostly disappears into sleep. She often buys something on her phone to cheer herself up. She divides what is left of the pay by all the hours the shift actually takes from her life, including travel and recovery. Her real hourly wage for night shifts is much lower than she thought. She politely says no to this one.

ask.q: Sunita is offered another extra night shift with good pay. What should she do before saying yes?
o: Subtract the extra costs and hours it brings, then decide
Accept immediately, since more pay is always better
Refuse, since all extra work is bad for her
ask.why: Pay is only half the picture. Night autos, food orders and a lost recovery day can shrink what she really earns. Saying yes or no on reflex skips that sum. Working out the real wage first shows whether the shift is truly worth it.

chapters.take: Your real wage is what remains after work's hidden costs and hours.

story.b: On a quiet afternoon off, Sunita downloads her UPI history for the last month and sorts it into groups in a notebook. Rent and fees. Groceries. Autos. Food orders. Phone and recharge. Gifts and family. Shopping. She promises herself not to judge, only to look. Some totals are what she expected. One is a shock. Food orders after night duty come to over six thousand rupees, more than her son's tuition. She also finds three small subscriptions she forgot she had. She does not scold herself. She just writes the totals neatly and circles the biggest ones. For the first time in years, she knows exactly where her month goes.

ask.q: Sunita's sister wants to track her spending but feels ashamed of her habits. What approach works best?
o: Track only the big expenses, since small ones do not matter
Record everything honestly, without judging herself, and look at the totals monthly
Wait until she has cut her bad spending, then start tracking
ask.why: Small spends often add up to the biggest surprises, so skipping them hides the truth. Waiting to be good first means never starting. Recording everything without shame lets her see clearly, and that awareness alone often shifts behaviour.

chapters.take: You cannot change spending you have never honestly looked at.

story.b: Sunita looks at each circled group and asks two questions. Did this give me joy worth the hours I spent earning it? Does it match what I care about? The food orders fail both. She eats them half asleep and barely remembers them. Her son's weekend swimming class at the sports complex passes easily. His face when he finished his first full length is worth every rupee. The phone she bought after a bad week fails. Her monthly film with her sister passes. So she changes a few things. On her day off she cooks a big batch of dal and rotis for night duty days. She cancels the forgotten subscriptions. Swimming and the films stay.

ask.q: Sunita spends a lot on two things: food orders and her son's swimming class. What should she do?
o: Cut both equally to save as much as possible
Keep both, since she works hard and deserves them
Ask which truly brought joy worth its cost and fits her values, then cut the other
ask.why: Cutting everything equally treats joy and waste the same, and keeping everything ignores what the numbers showed. Asking whether each was worth the hours lets her drop what disappoints, like half-eaten orders, and protect what matters, like her son's class.

chapters.take: Keep what is worth the hours. Quietly drop what is not.

story.b: One evening, Sunita writes a page titled enough. A rented two-room flat close to the hospital. Her son's education. A trip each year to her parents' village near Barabanki. No instalments for things she does not need. Some savings for emergencies, so one bad month does not frighten her. She realises she does not need most of the extra shifts to live this life. She drops one extra shift a week. With the money she now saves on orders and subscriptions, she starts a small monthly SIP, after a trusted advisor explains the basics and the risks. She knows it is a slow, long habit, not a quick win. But she can picture a day when her savings carry more of the load.

ask.q: Sunita's friend says enough is impossible because she always wants a bit more. What would help her most?
o: Write down what a life of enough looks like, in concrete terms
Earn as much as possible first and decide later
Match what richer relatives spend, so she does not fall behind
ask.why: Without a clear picture of enough, more always feels needed and the finish line keeps moving. Matching others ties her spending to their lives, not hers. Writing down what enough means for her makes saving purposeful, and over time growing savings can make work more of a choice.

chapters.take: Knowing what is enough turns saving into freedom, not sacrifice.

story.b: Six months later, on the twentieth of the month, Sunita checks her account and there is still money in it. Not a lot, but some, and it feels like breathing room. She works fewer extra shifts and sleeps better on her days off. The batch-cooked dal is now a Sunday ritual, and her son helps roll the rotis. She has not ordered food after night duty in weeks. The big TV is still in the shop near Hazratganj, and she does not miss it. On Sundays she sits by the pool at the sports complex, watching her son swim lengths. When she wants something new, she still asks herself one quiet question: how many hours is this?

chapters.take: Seeing money as hours of life helped her spend less and live more.
